problem: VLN research follows a train-once-deploy-once strategy, so agents finetuned on new environments catastrophically forget earlier ones. There is no benchmark or method for continual learning in VLN, and existing CL methods target single-step classification rather than sequential action prediction.
motivation: Deployed robots keep meeting new environments and must adapt without forgetting old ones. Standard CL methods (regularization, gradient projection, adapters) are designed for simple tasks and may not transfer to sequential, environment-dependent decision-making. Rehearsal looks promising, so the paper asks how to build and use the replay memory for navigation episodes.
key_idea: Formulate Continual VLN over sequential scene domains (I-CVLN and D-CVLN) and use rehearsal with two designs: Perplexity Replay, which keeps high action-perplexity episodes, and Episodic Self-Replay, which distills stored per-step action logits.
insight: Rehearsal beats regularization, gradient-projection and adapter methods, which fall below even the Vanilla baseline. Reversing the PerpR update (keeping low-perplexity episodes) drops I-CVLN SR from 28.9 to 27.1 and D-CVLN GP from 6.1 to 5.4, supporting the hard-episode assumption. In the ESR ablation, removing the logit-replay loss hurts more (SR 31.1 to 24.9) than removing the ground-truth replay loss (to 27.9), so step-level self-distillation is the main contributor. Larger memory generally helps.
method: CVLN formulation: agent trained sequentially on S scene domains (domain identity known in training, not at test); evaluated with the average over all domains after the final domain is learned (AvgSR/SPL/NE, AvgGP)
I-CVLN benchmark: English R2R+RxR episodes, 15,700 train episodes split into 20 scene domains (>600 episodes each), evaluated on 1,563 val-seen episodes
D-CVLN benchmark: CVDN dialogues, 4 scenes per domain giving 11 domains, 3,737 train episodes, 382 val episodes
Perplexity Replay (PerpR): computes Action Perplexity AP=exp(-1/N sum log P(a_i|v_i,I)) per episode; after each domain, adds high-AP episodes and evicts low-AP ones; loss L_D + L_M

Episodic Self-Replay (ESR): stores the per-step action logits of the model after each domain in memory (random/reservoir sampling); trains with an L2 logit-matching loss and student forcing that follows stored logits
Backbones: VLN-BERT with Oscar for I-CVLN; randomly initialized HAMT for D-CVLN; memory 500 episodes (~3%) for I-CVLN and 100 for D-CVLN

setting.backbone: VLN-BERT (Oscar) for I-CVLN; HAMT (random init) for D-CVLN; trained sequentially
setting.training_data: R2R+RxR English train episodes (15,700, 20 domains) for I-CVLN; CVDN train (3,737 episodes, 11 domains) for D-CVLN; replay memory of 500 / 100 episodes
setting.observation: panoramic RGB views with language instruction (I-CVLN) or dialogue history (D-CVLN)
setting.privileged: scene-domain identity during training (and AdapterCL selects adapters by perplexity at test)

numbers_note: Custom benchmarks; the validation set is the val-seen split. Joint upper bound: I-CVLN AvgSPL 40.1 / AvgSR 42.6 / AvgNE 7.1, D-CVLN AvgGP 8.1. Vanilla: 23.1 / 25.6 / 10.5 and 5.5.
results: ESR reaches AvgSR 31.9 and AvgSPL 28.2 on I-CVLN, and PerpR reaches AvgGP 6.1 on D-CVLN. These beat Random Replay (28.0 / 24.9 / 5.7) and Vanilla, and L2, A-GEM and AdapterCL fall below Vanilla. All methods remain well below the Joint upper bound (SR 42.6, GP 8.1).
limitations: Benchmarks are built from existing discrete-graph datasets (R2R/RxR/CVDN) rather than continuous environments, and the validation episodes are val-seen
Large gap remains to joint training, and results depend on replay memory size; the best method differs between I-CVLN and D-CVLN
Domain identity is needed during training, and the paper studies only one backbone per setting with high variance across curricula
